reports.title: REPORT OF FOREIGN PRIVATE ISSUER PURSUANT TO RULE 13a-16 OR 15d-16 UNDER THE SECURITIES EXCHANGE ACT OF 1934

lines: In exchange for committed capacity, the Company expects to pay $200.0 million of advance payments during the first half of calendar year 2027.

desk.headline: Revenue up 27% to $1.44bn and adjusted EPS of $0.52, both beats; Q3 revenue outlook of $1.54bn slightly above estimates
results: Revenue rose 27% to $1.44bn, above the company's own $1.38bn ±$50m guide; licence revenue jumped 50% to $773m while royalties grew 8% to $670m.
Adjusted EPS rose 33% to $0.52; GAAP diluted EPS fell to $0.12 from $0.22 as R&D rose to $857m and the prior year included a $128m non-operating gain.
Data centre royalties doubled from a year ago, while higher memory prices weighed on smartphone royalties.
Annualised contract value rose 12% to $1.79bn; adjusted free cash flow fell to $110m from $411m.
Cash and short-term investments stood at $3.6bn at 30 September.

guidance.summary: For the December quarter Arm expects revenue of $1.54bn ±$50m and adjusted EPS of $0.56 ±$0.04, with revenue slightly above the analysts' average reported by Reuters. No full-year range; it says it is more confident of up to $2bn of AGI CPU chip revenue over FY27–28.

points: Management put data centres at the centre of growth: Arm-based servers are expected to top 60% share at large cloud providers by end-2026.
Its own AGI CPU chip has orders running through 2027, with first commercial deliveries planned for the March quarter; CEO Rene Haas called $2bn "very achievable".
Arm says it worked with TSMC and other suppliers to secure materials for those chips.
Smartphone royalties were held back by memory prices; Arm-based PCs reached about a fifth of global shipments.
Spending keeps rising, led by R&D, with adjusted operating costs up 19%.
call.source: Shareholder letter (6-K Exhibit 99.2) and Reuters via Global Banking & Finance Review, 4 Nov 2026

watch: First AGI CPU deliveries in the March quarter and progress towards the $2bn target.
Smartphone royalties while memory prices stay high.
Cash flow and margins as R&D and chip-related spending grow.
